The further down on the periodic table you go, the bigger an atom gets. Similarly, the further to the right on the periodic table, the bigger an atom gets....sortof.

Within each group (s, p, d, or f), you add more protons to a nucleus. The additional protons will draw the electrons in closer and making the radius smaller. Looking at Potassium, it's outer orbital shell will be the S shell, which can hold a max of two electrons. Potassium will have one, and Calcium next to it will hold two. At first though you may say Calcium is bigger as it has more protons and more electrons. However, because the electrons are so small compared to the protons, the additional proton in Calcium will draw the two electrons closer to the nucleus and make the atom smaller. Continuing to the right, Scandium will start filling the d suborbital, which will have electrons further out and making the radius larger than both K and Ca.

bromine(Br) has more protons and neutrons than potassium (k). lets assume neither are ions because that could change the "size" of the atom. the atom's "size" is determined by its valance electrons. bromine has more electrons, those electrons are being pulled towards the stronger positive charge of its nucleus but they are also repelling each other as well as following the pauli exclusion principle. as such the electron cloud pushes out more.

electronegativity has a little to do with size, smaller atoms will be more electronegative, but also valence electrons play a crucial role in electronegativity (they are trying to form the octet). K has only one valence electron, so it is not very electronegative since it would be much easier to pass that electron off than to collect 7 more. Br has 7 valence electrons so is much more electronegative than K is.

smaller atoms are more electronegative because their positively charged nucleus is closer to the valence shell. this nucleus attracts the electrons. but the pauli exclusion principle and octets is more important when it comes to electronegativity.

an atom with more electrons will be larger because the electrons will push away from each other. this is also true of ions (negative ions are larger than positive ions).

I'm recapping a few things already said in other posts, but here goes:

Bromine and Potassium are both in the 4th period, but Bromine is a halogen and Potassium an alkali metal. They're about as far away from each other as you can get - so the teacher's question is most likely "Tell me why atomic radius increases as you move from metals to nonmetals" or something. Let's go with that.

  • Electron Shielding

As we move from bromine to the right, we add a proton to the nucleus each time. A proton has a charge of +1 and an electron has a charge of -1. If you add a proton and an electron to an atom, they should cancel out, right? Not quite. Remember that an electron exists in a fuzzy quantum cloud around the atom, sometimes in front of it and sometimes behind. It depends on the situation, but a valence electron usually cancels out only 30-60% of the proton's charge. This means that as protons go up, so does electronegativity.

Now potassium has 19 protons, and bromine has 35. That's a difference of 16 protons! When only 30-60% of their charge is getting canceled out, that means quite a bit of atomic charge is 'leaking' out through the electron cloud. Bromine and potassium were probably chosen because they'd have the greatest possible difference in their outer valence shell to demonstrate this.

  • Electron-electron Repulsion

So now remember that electrons are like "clouds" that repel each other. What are they going to do when they're more strongly attracted to a nucleus? Like quantum springs, they'll pack down closer to each other. Electric effects also depend on distance, so the closer they pack the more intensely they experience that electric effect anyway!

  • Ionization

In the image, bromine has an extra electron and potassium is missing one. Why does this matter? Well, this only compounds the existing issues. Potassium's missing electron means that it's got one less orbital adding to its size. There's less electron-electron repulsion, allowing the rest of them to pack down even closer to the nucleus. Bromine's extra electron means it's got one more orbital puffing its size up. There's also more electron-electron repulsion, forcing all the other electrons away from each other (and the nucleus) even more.
